analysis.one_liner: Blocks EPA carbon-pollution rules for power plants until carbon capture is proven economically feasible.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: introduced with 7 cosponsors in May 2013, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Power Subcommittee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped the EPA from finalizing any Clean Air Act rule limiting carbon dioxide emissions from coal- or gas-fired power plants — existing or new — unless the agency first determined that carbon capture and storage is the best way to cut those emissions and three of four specified federal officials reported the technology to be technologically and economically feasible [S2] [S3]. It would also have barred the EPA from putting coal-fired steam units and cleaner gas combined-cycle units in the same regulatory category, which would prevent one standard from being stretched across both kinds of plants [S2] [S3]. The bill received no action beyond committee referral [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be coal mining companies and the operators of coal- and gas-fired power plants, which would have been shielded from federal carbon-pollution limits for as long as carbon capture remained too expensive to meet the bill's economic test [S2] [S3]. Coal-producing regions and power-plant-dependent communities would also have gained from avoided plant-retirement pressure [S1].

how_it_helps.text: The bill sets a strict precondition for any EPA carbon rule for power plants: carbon capture and storage must be both the EPA's chosen best system of emission reduction and certified as technologically and economically feasible in a Federal Register report signed by at least three of four federal officials — the EIA Administrator, the Comptroller General, the Director of the National Energy Technology Laboratory, and the Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology [S2] [S3].

The bill's economic-feasibility definition is demanding: a plant using carbon capture must be projected to earn more revenue over its lifetime than it costs, including the energy needed to capture, compress, transport, and store the carbon dioxide [S3].
It also prevents the EPA from regulating coal-fired utility steam units and gas combined-cycle units as a single combined category, keeping the two on separate regulatory tracks [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, ordinary people would have borne the cost of years of continued carbon and air pollution from coal- and gas-fired power plants, since the feasibility condition would function as a de facto freeze on EPA carbon standards. Downwind communities and future generations would absorb the health and climate consequences, and federal climate policy would be stalled regardless of what the science or economics showed.

drawbacks.text: Because the bill ties the EPA's hands until carbon capture passes a strict lifetime-cost test, and that technology has not been deployed economically at power-plant scale, the provision would effectively bar — not merely delay — carbon standards for existing coal plants, leaving their emissions unregulated under section 111 of the Clean Air Act [S2] [S3].

The economic-feasibility definition counts only the private revenue and cost of the plant, ignoring the public health and environmental costs of continued emissions, so the feasibility test could be met or failed without any reference to the damage the pollution causes [S3].

Supporters' honest cost: coal-state members argued that forcing carbon rules before carbon capture is proven would shutter plants and raise electricity rates in coal-dependent regions; the bill traded that near-term regional economic risk for indefinite pollution from the affected plants [S1] [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For coal mining and coal-plant operators the bill was close to pure gain: it used an unmet technological condition to lock out carbon regulation. The cost would fall on everyone else — prolonged carbon emissions and delayed air-quality progress with no offsetting benefit. This is a bill whose protection of one industry comes directly at the public's expense, and its early death in committee prevented that outcome.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, and then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, and never moved again — no hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David McKinley introduced the bill on May 23, 2013, joined on introduction by Reps. Rahall, Capito, Johnson of Ohio, Olson, Latta, Griffith, and Peterson [S3] [S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on May 24, 2013 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote — is recorded for the bill before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5] [S1].
The bill drew 7 cosponsors: 5 Republicans and 2 Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill never advanced, so coal-plant operators got no legislative shield from carbon standards; the EPA's Clean Air Act authority over power-plant emissions was left untouched by Congress, which is the outcome ordinary people would want if the rule's merits were ever tested.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal operators gained nothing; EPA authority untouched

for.name: Rep. David B. McKinley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar final EPA carbon rules for power plants until carbon capture is certified as technologically and economically feasible.

for.name: 7 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at or near introduction.

against.name: Rep. Fred Upton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup or sent it to the floor; the bill stayed with the subcommittee after referral.

against.name: House Energy and Power Subcommittee
against.role: Subcommittee of the Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 24, 2013, and took no recorded action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: EPA (Obama administration)
against.role: Federal regulator whose carbon rules the bill targeted
against.what_they_did: Was moving to set carbon dioxide standards for power plants under Clean Air Act section 111, the rules this bill was written to block.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was mostly Republican (5 of 7), with the two Democratic cosponsors coming from coal- and rural-district members; no floor vote ever occurred to test the parties more broadly [S4].

industries.industry: Coal mining and coal-fired power plant operators
industries.note: The bill would have blocked EPA carbon rules for existing and new coal plants until carbon capture passes a strict economic-feasibility test, sparing operators large compliance and retirement costs. The public pays instead through continued carbon and air pollution from those same plants.

The bill also covers all fossil-fired units and bars the EPA from combining coal steam units with gas combined-cycle units in one regulatory category, keeping gas plants on a separate, potentially less stringent track. The benefit is smaller than for coal but comes from the same carve-out logic.

industries.industry: Electric utility ratepayers in coal-dependent regions
industries.note: Supporters' stated concern was avoiding electricity rate increases and plant closures in coal-dependent areas. That near-term regional benefit is real but is paired with the cost of indefinite emissions for everyone else.
